use /lib
from /scope/application import ApplicationScope

export scope EdgeReleasesScope:
    concept: {EdgeReleasesConcept}

concept EdgeReleasesConcept:
    pitch:
        Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and
        macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can
        download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

    shape: {EdgeReleasesShape}

shape EdgeReleasesShape:
    description:
        A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository,
        `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release
        for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull
        requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push,
        for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of
        whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

    version:
        An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's
        sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds,
        counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on
        main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same
        commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the
        whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.

        The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the
        application knows its own version, and so is the repository it is
        published from, as `owner/name`, which marks it as an edge build that
        can update itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's
        machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it, and no repository.

    builds:
        The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run
        side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

        - Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
        - Windows, x86_64
        - macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

        Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs
        whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as
        Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the
        repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in
        `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build
        needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no
        console of its own, as the @{ApplicationScope} says.

        The code compiles, its tests included, on each of the three
        platforms, with no compiler warnings on any of them. What differs
        between platforms, as a system call whose signature differs between
        Linux and macOS, or an import only one platform uses, is written for
        each platform it builds on, and gated to the platforms that use it,
        so nothing is unused or mistyped on another. No deprecated function
        is called where its replacement is available. Each job denies
        warnings in its build and its tests, so a warning fails the job, and
        no edge release is published, as for an error. A build script's own
        notes, as one saying where the default prompts were taken from, are
        not compiler warnings, and don't fail it.

    publishing:
        Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is
        published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled
        "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the
        latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash,
        linked to the commit, and its message's first line.

        Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary
        alone, named for the version and the platform:

        - `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

        The binaries are not signed or notarized.

        If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit,
        so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows
        which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when
        a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing
        more for it and succeeds.

        Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one
        before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on
        main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the
        permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents,
        and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its
        own.

content.text:
I've added test rules to the spec that cover this failure and the other ways tests commonly break across Linux, macOS and Windows. I couldn't run the tests myself: the code isn't mounted in this spec run, so the code step has to run the full suite from scratch. `piton check` reports no problems, the file is formatted, and `piton build` succeeds. I confirmed the new rules in the refreshed reference.

**Likely cause of this failure:** the runner path (`/Users/runner/…`) shows it failed on macOS. The test opens the send menu, then looks for `send-option` 1, the Queue option. The elements actually there include the `send-options` button but no menu options, so the menu never opened. The spec says the shortcut is **Cmd**+Shift+Enter on macOS, so a test that presses Ctrl+Shift+Enter does nothing there. That's my best guess from the output, not confirmed by running it.

**Test rules now in the spec.** Every test must pass on all three platforms, on a fresh runner, run in parallel and in any order:
- **Shortcuts:** pressed as the platform binds them, Cmd on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere.
- **Paths and line endings:** paths are built with the platform's separators and compared as the platform compares them, and `\r\n` vs `\n` is ignored. These typically break on Windows.
- **Nothing taken from the machine:** no piton, Podman, harness, network, home folder or config folder. The build output confirms the runners have no piton. Tests fake what they need in their own temporary folder. Git is the one exception, configured per test with a name and email.
- **Waiting:** tests wait for background work with generous timeouts, never fixed sleeps.
- **Element ids:** the ids a test uses must exist under that scope in that frame, for example a menu's options only once the menu is open.

## What changed in the spec, and the anchors the code should follow

- **`EdgeReleasesShape.builds` (new paragraph and list):** the rules above.

**For the code step:**
1. **`chat_input::tests::queue_option_and_editing_a_queued_prompt`:**
   - Press the platform's shortcut, using the same secondary-modifier binding the app uses, so it's Cmd on macOS.
   - Confirm the menu is open before looking for `send-option` 1.
   - If the menu's element ids have changed, update the test to match the interface as specced.
2. **Run `cargo test` from scratch and fix every failure.** Then check the whole suite for these patterns:
   - Hard-coded `ctrl-` keystrokes
   - `/`-joined path literals compared as text
   - Line-ending-sensitive comparisons
   - Dependence on piton, Podman, a harness, the network, `$HOME` or the config folder
   - Unconfigured git identity
   - Fixed sleeps

   Fix any of these even where they currently pass on Linux.
3. **Keep CI's warning settings from last turn,** `-D warnings` for both build and tests.
